title: 1917: the Russian Revolution
subtitle: February to October, in a calendar thirteen days behind
summary:
Eight months in which a three-hundred-year monarchy, the government that replaced it, and the war all came apart in the same city. It begins with a bread queue on the Vyborg side and ends with a committee in a girls' school taking the telephone exchange. The map works at two scales that are three orders of magnitude apart: the Russian Empire, where an army of eleven million was dissolving, and about six kilometres of Petrograd, where everything that is remembered actually happened.

Russia kept the Julian calendar until February 1918, thirteen days behind the West. That is why the February Revolution happened in March and the October Revolution in November, and it is the instrument this pack is built around: every instant stored here is Gregorian, and every date a reader sees carries the Russian date beside it.

branches.summary: The eight months as they ran: the bread queues, the garrison changing sides, the abdication, dual power, Lenin's return, the July Days, Kornilov, and the night of 25 October (O.S.).

rail.note: This pack's rail is the scheduled passenger express carrying individuals - Lenin's carriage from Zurich to the Finland Station, the imperial train from Mogilev to Pskov - and not an army entraining, which is what the 1914 default (15/30 km/h) is calibrated on. Merridale reconstructs the April journey stage by stage from the German, Swedish and Russian records: the party covered 500-800 km between the stops the record names, which is 15-27 km/h of straight-line displacement including border halts and a night in Stockholm. 30 is that sustained figure rounded; 50 is what a through express of 1917 could make over a leg without stopping, which nothing in this pack reaches.
